subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: If y = xʸ, show that dy/dx = y²/(x(1 − log y)) = y²/(x(1 − y log x)).

mark_split.label: Differentiate both sides with respect to x
Show the two printed forms agree

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IB (2026-27 edition), book p.200, chapter 9 DIFFERENTIATION, Short Answer question 3. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the volume prints a CHAPTER-level marks banner (8M + 4M + 2 × 2M = 16M) but no per-step allocation on any answer. The split follows the shape this bank uses for a Maths-1B Section B question. This book prints almost no exam-appearance years, so appearances[] is empty — the chapter has long been examined, we simply have no sourced years for this question. Paper position: Maths-1B Section B runs Q11 to Q18 at 4 marks each, answer any 6 of 8, under the 2026-27 pattern. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. The mathematics was checked independently before writing: y was found numerically from y = xʸ at x = 1.2 (y = 1.25773454) and x = 1.1 (y = 1.11178201), and BOTH printed forms of dy/dx agree with a central difference quotient there (1.71048079 and 1.25687377). The question offers the answer in two forms, so the equivalence is authored as a scoring step rather than a remark.

recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this — say what you do first, and how the two printed forms of the answer are connected.

steps.label: Take logarithms of both sides
steps.margin_note: First mark. Keep this line visible on the page — the last step needs it again to change one printed form into the other.
lines: Take logarithms on both sides (log means logₑ throughout):

recall.must_convey: That logarithms are taken on both sides, giving log y = y log x.
accept: take log on both sides so the index comes down
log y equals y log x
logarithm both sides because y is in the power
rendu vaipula log teeste log y equals y log x
apply log to bring the exponent in front
start with logarithmic differentiation

steps.why: y appears both on its own and as the index, so no single rule applies to y = xʸ directly. Taking logarithms brings the index down and turns the right side into a product of two functions of x, which the product rule can differentiate.
common_mistakes: Writing log(xʸ) as (log x)ʸ instead of y log x.
Treating xʸ as a power of x and writing y·xʸ⁻¹, which is only valid when the index is a constant.
steps.memory_tip: One line, two uses: log y = y log x opens the question and closes it. It also connects the two printed forms of the answer.

steps.label: Differentiate both sides with respect to x
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Two dy/dx terms must appear — one from the left side by the chain rule, one from the right side by the product rule. Missing either one loses this mark.
lines: Differentiate with respect to x. The left side needs the chain rule and the right side the product rule, because y is a function of x.

accept: differentiate log y as one by y into dy by dx
product rule on y log x gives dy by dx log x plus y by x
both sides differentiate with respect to x
y log x ki product rule apply cheyyali
one by y dy by dx equals log x dy by dx plus y by x
y is a function of x so the chain rule is needed on the left

steps.why: y is a function of x, so log y differentiates to (1/y)(dy/dx) and not to 1/y. On the right, y log x is a product of two functions of x, so both factors must be differentiated in turn.
common_mistakes: Differentiating log y as 1/y and leaving out the factor dy/dx.
Treating y as a constant in y log x, which gives only (y/x) and loses the second dy/dx term.
steps.memory_tip: Every time y is differentiated, a dy/dx comes with it. Count the dy/dx terms in this line: there must be exactly two.

steps.label: Collect the dy/dx terms
steps.margin_note: Third mark. The bracket (1/y − log x) is combined over the denominator y before dividing. Doing that in one written line is what makes the y² appear in the numerator.
lines: Bring the dy/dx terms to one side:

recall.must_convey: That the dy/dx terms are collected and rearranged to give dy/dx = y²/(x(1 − y log x)).
accept: take dy by dx common on one side
one by y minus log x becomes one minus y log x over y
dy by dx equals y squared by x into one minus y log x
dy by dx common teesi y ni pyki teesukoni divide cheyyali
shift the second dy by dx term to the left
cross multiply to get y squared in the numerator

steps.why: Both dy/dx terms must sit on the same side before dy/dx can be taken out as a common factor. Writing 1/y − log x as the single fraction (1 − y log x)/y is what turns the y on the right into y² after dividing.
common_mistakes: Leaving the answer as (y/x)/(1/y − log x) without clearing the inner fraction.
Getting y instead of y² in the numerator by dividing rather than multiplying by y.
steps.memory_tip: The y² is not an extra square — it is the y from y/x multiplied by the y released when 1/y − log x is written as one fraction.

steps.label: Show the two printed forms agree
steps.margin_note: Last mark. The question prints the answer twice, so the examiner expects the link between the two brackets to be written down, not assumed. It is a single substitution from step 1.
lines: From step 1, log y = y log x
So the bracket 1 − y log x can be written as 1 − log y

lines.text: ∴ dy/dx = y²/(x(1 − y log x)) = y²/(x(1 − log y))

recall.must_convey: That log y = y log x is substituted into the bracket, so the two printed forms are the same expression.
accept: since log y equals y log x the two brackets are equal
replace y log x by log y in the denominator
both forms are the same because of the first line
log y equals y log x kabatti rendu forms okate
substitute back from the logarithm step
one minus y log x is one minus log y

steps.why: The two printed answers are not two results. They are one result written with the bracket in two ways, and the relation taken in step 1 is exactly what converts one into the other, so the equivalence costs one line.
common_mistakes: Giving only one of the two forms when the question asks for both.
Trying to prove the equivalence from the original relation y = xʸ again instead of using the logarithm line already written.
steps.memory_tip: Go back to the first line to finish the last one: wherever y log x appears, log y may be written instead.

insider_note: Take logarithms to get log y = y log x, then differentiate — the right side needs the product rule because y depends on x. Both printed forms follow from y = xʸ.
